1394.title: Accepting the will
1394.hook: bhaana is sweet acceptance of what the Lord sends
1394.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of bhaana mannana, accepting the Lord's will, especially in loss; the shabad tera keeya meetha laagai is often sung in kirtan, and Sikhs recall it in connection with Guru Arjan's martyrdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, death without fear: whoever has come will go, and remembering the fearless One loosens fear's grip. Your line was unafraid.

Tera keeya meetha laagai. A short line from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raag Asa: your doing seems sweet to me. Sikhs sing it in kirtan, and it's easy to hum without hearing how bold it is. It doesn't say your doing is easy, or what I wanted. It says sweet. About whatever comes. Tradition ties the line to Guru Arjan's own last days, which were anything but sweet. Today's word is the inner turn that makes a line like that possible: bhaana.
screen: `TERA KEEYA MEETHA LAAGAI.` → `YOUR DOING SEEMS SWEET TO ME.` → `BHAANA.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Bhaana is the will of the Lord, what pleases the Lord, the way things come to us; you met it early on this path, in an Ardas said in grief. Sikhs speak of bhaana mannana: accepting the will. It sits close to Hukam. Hukam is the order itself; bhaana is that order arriving in your own life, on an ordinary day, as news you didn't ask for. Second, the line in full. In paraphrase: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Lord's Name. Not a different outcome. The Name. The prayer turns from changing what happened to staying close to the One it came from. Third, the hardest part. Tradition says Guru Arjan was tortured in Lahore and died there, and that through it he kept repeating this very line. Sikhs remember that as bhaana at its hardest: not a calm man in a calm room, but a man in agony, still saying sweet. Fourth, what bhaana is not. It isn't giving up. The same tradition tells how his son, the Sixth Guru, took up arms. Sikhs feed the hungry, stand against injustice, go to the doctor, fix what can be fixed. Bhaana is the heart's stance toward what has already come, not an excuse to stop acting on what can still change. It's taking what arrived, even bitter, and refusing to let it push the Lord out of the room.
screen: `BHAANA: THE WILL, ARRIVING.` · `NOT A NEW OUTCOME, BUT THE NAME.` · `GURU ARJAN, STILL SAYING SWEET.` · `NOT A SHRUG; STILL ACTING.` · then, large: `TERA KEEYA MEETHA LAAGAI.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been resisting that you truly cannot change: not an injustice you could act on, but something that has simply happened, a delay, a no, a body slower than it was. On the in-breath, name it; on the out-breath, try the word accepted, and see if any part of you can loosen. Sweet may be too far today; lighter is enough, and if you pray, you can hum the Guru's line.
Bhaana. The will of the Lord, as it arrives in a life; bhaana mannana is accepting it, sweetly, while still doing what can be done. Today's word.
Your line: his will. Not a shrug: acceptance, with hands still working. See you on the path tomorrow.

1395.title: Humility in practice
1395.hook: nimrata is not weakness; it is strength that doesn't need to show
1395.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of nimrata, humility, as a core virtue, practiced in seva such as cleaning shoes and serving langar, and in bowing before the Guru Granth Sahib on entering the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhaana: the will as it arrives, met without pushing the Lord out of the room. Your line was his will.

Who is the strongest person at a family argument? Not the loudest. Often it's the one who could win, who has the facts and the sharp line ready, and lets it go. That's real strength, even though nothing was shown. Now picture a market stall, old style: a balance scale, two pans hanging from a beam. Something goes in each pan, and one side sinks. Guru Nanak turns that scale into a teaching about people: nimrata, and the side that goes down.
screen: `THE ONE WHO COULD WIN, AND DOESN'T.` → `TWO PANS ON A BEAM.` → `NIMRATA.`

segments.voice: First, the line, which you met early on this path. In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of all virtue and goodness. In the original, mithat neevee: sweetness and lowliness. Neevee is the posture of bending low. Second, the tree. In the same passage he describes the simmal, the silk-cotton tree: tall, straight as an arrow, impressive from far away. Birds come hoping for fruit and leave disappointed; its fruit is tasteless and its leaves are no use. All that height, and nothing to give. Third, the scale. Then the turn, in paraphrase: when weighed on the balance, the side that bows down is the heavier. That's the strength hidden in nimrata. The pan that sinks isn't the weak one. It sinks because it has more in it. Fourth, a warning, so nobody fakes it. The passage goes on, in paraphrase: the wrongdoer bows down even lower, like the hunter stalking a deer. Bowing can be a crouch before the pounce. So the Guru isn't praising the look of humility. He's praising the weight. Humility in practice isn't putting yourself down or saying you're nothing. It's having something real and not needing it seen. The one at the argument who lets the point go isn't losing. They're the heavier pan.
screen: `MITHAT NEEVEE: SWEETNESS AND LOWLINESS.` · `THE TALL TREE WITH NOTHING TO GIVE.` · `THE SIDE THAT BOWS IS HEAVIER.` · `THE HUNTER BOWS TOO: NOT THE LOOK.` · then, large: `STRENGTH THAT DOESN'T SHOW.`

segments.voice: Think of one small contest coming up: the last word in a chat, who picks the restaurant, whose idea gets credit. Picture yourself letting it go, quietly, without a sigh, and on each breath let the weight sink like the heavier pan. If a voice inside says but I was right, let it say so, and let the breath carry on.
Humility in practice. Nimrata: not weakness or self-contempt, but strength that doesn't need to be seen; on the Guru's scale, the side that bows is the heavier one. Today's word.
Your line: strength that doesn't show. The side that bows is the heavier. Until tomorrow.

1396.title: Contentment, not complacency
1396.hook: santokh is peace with what is, while still acting
1396.howItsDone: Sikhs count santokh, contentment, among the core virtues and pair it with kirat karni, honest work, and vand chhakna, sharing what is earned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, humility in practice: on Guru Nanak's scale, the side that bows is the heavier one. Your line was strength that doesn't show.

Morning on the bank of the Ravi, and a man walks out with the farmers to work the soil. Tradition says this is Guru Nanak in his later years, at Kartarpur, the town where he settled after his long journeys. The teacher of the Japji, out plowing. He could have sat and received offerings. Instead, the story goes, he worked the land, and the community ate together from what it grew. That picture holds today's word in both hands: a deep peace with what is, and a plow still moving.

First, the word. Santokh: contentment, enough, the end of the restless more. You've met it often on this path, and a few days ago Asa di Var put it in a chariot: in Satjug, contentment was the chariot. Second, why it matters. In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: without contentment, no one is satisfied; like dreams, every wish and every effort comes to nothing. Notice the target: not wanting things, but being satisfied. A person can get everything on the list and still feel hungry, because the list was never the hunger. Third, the trap on the other side. Contentment could slide into complacency: I'm fine, the world's fine, why bother. The Gurus close that door. In a salok, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: the one who eats what they earn by their own effort, and gives some of it from their own hand, Nanak, that one recognizes the way. Earn. Give. Both are verbs. Contentment isn't a couch. Fourth, the field again. Guru Nanak at Kartarpur, as tradition tells it, is content enough to need no throne, active enough to plow. So santokh doesn't ask a student to stop studying, a worker to stop asking for a fair wage, or anyone to stop fighting injustice. It asks them to do all that without the gnawing. Complacency stops the hands. Contentment only quiets the hunger.
screen: `SANTOKH: THE END OF THE RESTLESS MORE.` · `WITHOUT CONTENTMENT, NO ONE IS FULL.` · `EARN BY EFFORT, GIVE FROM YOUR HAND.` · `QUIET THE HUNGER, NOT THE HANDS.` · then, large: `CONTENT AND WORKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're working toward: a goal, a project, a skill. On the in-breath, say inside: this is enough, right now; on the out-breath: and I'll keep working. Let both sit side by side, like the farmer's peace and the farmer's plow.
Contentment. Santokh: peace with what is, the end of the gnawing for more, held together with honest work and sharing. Today's word.
Your line: content and working. Peace with what is, and a plow still moving. Go gently.

1397.title: Compassion in practice
1397.hook: daya is the mother of dharma in the Japji
1397.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of daya, compassion, as a core virtue and express it in seva: serving langar, caring for the sick and helping those in need, whoever they are.

segments.voice: Yesterday, contentment: santokh quiets the hunger for more, but not the hands. Your line was content and working.

An old Indian picture of the world: the earth rests on the back of a great bull. It holds everything up. Solid, simple, done. Then someone asks the question a child would ask: and what is the bull standing on? In the Japji, Guru Nanak asks it. In paraphrase: how much weight is on that bull, and what holds it up from below? He doesn't throw the old picture away. He opens it up, and puts something surprising inside. Today: compassion in practice.
screen: `THE EARTH ON A BULL'S BACK.` → `WHAT IS THE BULL STANDING ON?` → `COMPASSION IN PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: First, the answer, in the sixteenth pauri of the Japji. In paraphrase: the bull is dharma, the son of compassion; it is contentment that patiently holds the earth in its place. In the original, dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot. The bull is righteous living, dharma. And dharma has a mother: daya, compassion. Yesterday's santokh shows up too, as the thread that keeps it steady. Second, what that order means. Compassion comes first. Rules, duties, right conduct: all of it is born from caring. If dharma loses its mother, it becomes rules that can be kept coldly, even cruelly. If it keeps her, the rules stay warm. Third, the same pairing, in a salok you met early on this path. In Asa di Var, offered a ritual sacred thread, Guru Nanak describes the only thread he'd wear. In paraphrase: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, self-restraint the knots, and truth the twist; that is the thread for the soul, and if you have it, put it on me. Compassion again sits at the bottom, the raw cotton everything is spun from. Fourth, in practice. Compassion here isn't a mood. It's what moves a hand: a langar ladle, a meal carried to a neighbor, a hard truth said gently instead of cruelly. It isn't softness either; a Sikh may stand firm against wrong and still let compassion set the tone. When a rule and a person seem to pull in different directions, ask the mother before you ask the son.
screen: `THE BULL IS DHARMA, SON OF COMPASSION.` · `RULES BORN FROM CARING STAY WARM.` · `THE THREAD: COMPASSION THE COTTON.` · `COMPASSION MOVES A HAND.` · then, large: `DHAUL DHARAM DAIAA KAA POOT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you'll see or talk to today: someone tired, maybe, or difficult, or easy to overlook. Breathe in and ask what it's like to be them today; breathe out and let a little of the answer reach you. Then let one small act that would help them come clear.
Compassion in practice. Daya: in the Japji, the mother of dharma; right conduct is born from caring, and caring shows up as something done. Today's word.
Your line: compassion first. In the Japji, dharma's mother is daya, compassion. See you tomorrow.

1398.title: Love, the path
1398.hook: love is the path the Tenth Guru said finds the Lord
1398.howItsDone: The Tav Prasad Swayye is among the morning prayers Sikhs recite, and the line on love, jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio, is sung in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion in practice: in the Japji, the bull is dharma, and dharma's mother is daya. Your line was compassion first.

A heron stands in shallow water at the edge of a pond. Perfectly still. One leg tucked up, eyes half closed, neck curved like a monk bowing in prayer. From the bank it looks perfectly at peace. Then a fish swims near, and the stillness ends in a flash. It was never meditating. It was waiting for lunch. Guru Gobind Singh, the Tenth Guru, used that bird in a verse. He asked what all our holy-looking stillness is worth, and gave one plain answer to everyone listening: prem.
screen: `A HERON, STILL AS A MONK.` → `WAITING FOR A FISH.` → `PREM.`

segments.voice: First, the heron. In the Tav Prasad Swayye, which Sikhs recite among their morning prayers, the Tenth Guru asks, in paraphrase: what does it matter if you shut your eyes and sit like a heron in meditation? He goes on through other outward feats: wandering from sea to sea to bathe, losing this world and the next along the way. Each can look holy from the bank. Each can be a heron. Second, the answer, a line you met early on this path: jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio. In paraphrase: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen: only those who have loved have found the Lord. The word is prem: love. Not ritual first. Not display first. Love. Third, love has a price. Guru Nanak said it too, in a salok kept near the end of the Granth. In paraphrase: if you long to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm; once you set foot on this path, give your head and don't hesitate. That's not soft romance. It's love that costs everything and doesn't look back. Fourth, an ordinary day. Prem changes the question under a practice. Not, did I pray long enough, or did I look devout, but, was there love in it? A Sikh can recite every bani and still be a heron. Someone can stumble through one line with a full heart and be found. This isn't the Guru throwing out discipline; he wrote prayers Sikhs recite in the morning. It's the Guru naming what the discipline is for.
screen: `THE HERON: HOLY FROM THE BANK.` · `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND THE LORD.` · `YOUR HEAD ON YOUR PALM.` · `WAS THERE LOVE IN IT?` · then, large: `JIN PREM KEEO TIN HEE PRABH PAAEIO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you love but rarely say it to: a parent, a sibling, an old friend, a child who's grown. Let their face stay with each in-breath, and on each out-breath send them whatever love is there. If you pray, you can hold them before the Lord.
Prem. Love; in the Tenth Guru's swayya, the path that finds the Lord, beneath every ritual and every outward show. Today's word.
Your line: those who loved, found. Not the heron's stillness, but a full heart. That's today, done.

1399.title: Truth, lived again
1399.hook: truth in speech and truth in conduct
1399.howItsDone: Sikhs hold truthful living, sach aachaar, as central to the path, and the line 'truth is high, but higher still is truthful living' from Sri Raag is quoted in Sikh teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prem: the heron looks holy, but only those who have loved have found the Lord. Your line was those who loved, found.

On my way. A text, sent from a couch, shoes still off. Nobody would call it a lie, exactly. Nothing in it is false in a way a court would care about. And yet something in it isn't true. The words point one direction and the person points another. This path has met sat, truth, many times: in the Mool Mantar, in the Mundavani's plate, in the Japji's opening. Today the Gurus press on the gap between the message and the couch. Truth, lived again.
screen: `ON MY WAY.` → `SENT FROM THE COUCH.` → `TRUTH, LIVED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the ladder, a line you met early on this path and worth climbing again. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak says: sachahu orai sabh ko, upar sach aachaar. In paraphrase: truth is higher than everything; higher still is truthful living. Truth is at the top, and the Guru puts one more rung above it. Not a truer idea. A truer life. Aachaar is conduct, the way a person actually behaves. Second, how truth is known. In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak gives a list, in paraphrase: one is known as true only when the truth is in the heart; then the filth of falsehood leaves, and the body is washed clean. The list goes on: loving the truth, taking true teaching, compassion to living beings, and giving. Truth here isn't only accurate words. It's a heart and a set of habits. Third, the two kinds side by side. Truth in speech: not saying what isn't so. Truth in conduct: being what you say. On my way, sent from the couch, barely scrapes past the first and fails the second. And plenty of sentences that aren't lies at all still fail the second: I'll pray for you, never prayed. Let's get coffee, never meant. Fourth, small promises. The Guru's ladder makes the smallest promise matter. A truthful life isn't built from grand vows. It's built from returning the call you said you'd return, showing up at the time you named. Each kept promise is a rung on that ladder.

Truth. Sat, which the Gurus honor in speech and, higher still, in conduct: sach aachaar, a life that matches its words. Today's word.
Your line: truth in conduct. A life that matches its words, one kept promise at a time. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1400.title: Anger, the burning thief
1400.hook: krodh burns the one who holds it; righteous anger is guided by compassion
1400.howItsDone: Sikhs name krodh, anger, among the five thieves, kaam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankar, and meet them through Naam Simran, the remembrance of the Lord, and the company of the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, truth: high, and higher still, truthful living. Your line was truth in conduct.

A coal, picked up bare-handed to throw at someone. Before it ever reaches them, whose hand is already burning? The Guru Granth Sahib names anger, krodh, among the five thieves living inside the body, the thieves you met early on this path. This one doesn't break in. It flares up from inside, and the first thing it burns is the one holding it. Yet the Gurus also spoke fiercely against cruelty. So which is it? Today: anger, and the second before it.
screen: `A COAL IN A BARE HAND.` → `KRODH, THE BURNING THIEF.` → `ANGER.`

segments.voice: First, Guru Arjan speaks to anger directly. In one of his saloks in the Granth he addresses it like a person. In paraphrase: O anger, root of strife, compassion never rises in you. Then, the saloks go on, it takes people over and makes them dance to its tune. It doesn't just add heat. It pushes compassion out of the room. Remember the Japji's bull a few days ago: dharma is the son of compassion. Anger shoves the mother out of her chair. Second, Farid's answer. In paraphrase: Farid, answer evil with good; don't fill your mind with anger. Then your body won't fall sick, and you'll gain everything. Notice the body. Farid knows anger wears down the one who holds it first. Third, the other anger. The Gurus were not quiet in the face of wrong. Guru Nanak cried out against the cruelty of an invading army; we heard that protest days ago. The difference is what steers it. Krodh is anger for me: my pride hurt, my plan blocked. The fierceness the Gurus show is for others, and it's guided by compassion, not by the thief. Fourth, the gap. Anger is fast. The tradition slows it with remembering, Simran, and in plain terms, a breath. One breath before the word. One breath before the send button. In that gap, compassion gets a chance to come back to its chair. Back to the coal: one breath can be long enough to notice it's in your own hand, and set it down.
screen: `ARJAN: ANGER, ROOT OF STRIFE.` · `FARID: ANSWER EVIL WITH GOOD.` · `FIERCE FOR OTHERS, GUIDED BY COMPASSION.` · `ONE BREATH BEFORE THE WORD.` · then, large: `BREATHE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing that reliably irritates you, a slow driver, a certain tone, a dish left in the sink, and let a little of the heat come. Notice where it lands in your body: jaw, chest, hands. Then take one slow breath, all the way in and out, before you think a single word about it, and watch what the heat does when it's given breaths instead of words.
Anger. Krodh, one of the five thieves: it burns the one who holds it and pushes compassion out; the fierceness the Gurus honor is guided by compassion. Today's word.
Your line: breathe first. One breath is room enough for compassion to come back. See you tomorrow.
